title: CHAPTER SIX. On the end of this world; heavens pass by free omnipotence, not natural cause
english: CHAPTER SIX. On the end of this world.

From the state of the separated soul there follows the end of this world, by which the heavens (Enchiridion chapter 91) will pass away with a great noise not from a natural cause but from the free determination and omnipotence of their Creator; the elements burning with heat will be dissolved, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.

title: Names of the end; this world began and will end; against Didymus on three worlds
english: It is called συντέλεια τοῦ αἰῶνος, the consummation of this age (Matthew 13:40 and 18:20); τέλος, end (Matthew 24:6, 14); harvest (Matthew 13:39 and Revelation 14:15–16 and Joel 3:13). This world, as it had a beginning, so also will have an end (Revelation 21:1; 2 Peter 3:5, 6, 7, 8, 12).

Nor is Didymus to be approved here, in his exposition on the canonical epistles, observing that mention is made here of a threefold world — of the ancient or past (verse 6), of the present (verse 7), and of the future after this one (verse 13) — which things he thinks were sprinkled into this epistle by heretics dreaming of several creations and periods of worlds. But this conjecture deceived him. For that Peter says the world perished by the flood sufficiently indicates that he is not speaking of three worlds diverse in essence, as the followers of Origen thoughtn thought, but only pointing out that just as this world once orrupted by water, so the same will sometime perish by fire.

title: Christians confess the end; Porphyry mocks; against Plato, Xenophanes, Aristotle, Averroes on eternity
english: And indeed this dogma has always been among the things confessed among Christians, whom therefore Porphyry mocks, as Augustine witnesses (City of God book 20, chapter 24), following Plato, who in the Timaeus hands down that the world began but will not perish. Others also withdrew further, as Xenophanes, who thought the world neither began nor will cease, as Plutarch is author in On the Opinions of the Philosophers book 2, chapter 4, and that long before Plato. For Xenophanes lived around the sixtieth Olympiad, that is, in the times of Cyrus and Tarquinius Superbus. Aristotle with great effort defends this sentence of Xenophanes (Physics book 8 and On the Heavens). Averroes defends Aristotle tooth and nail in his first disputation On the Eternity of the World, where he answers Algazel's solutions.

title: Fire is proper, not mere metaphor for wrath vs Puccius; Augustine on conflagration; Magius; starry heaven disputed
english: But fire is thought to be taken by metaphor for divine wrath and judgment by Franciscus Puccius of Filidino, as Nicolaus Serarius the Mainz Jesuit notes (book 1 against Puccius, chapter 2, and book 2, chapter 2): yet that it is taken properly is argued by this, that it is said that as it formerly perished by water, so on that day it will perish by fire. Hence Augustine (City of God book 20, chapter 16): Then, he says, the figure of this world will pass away by the conflagration of worldly fires, just as it was done by the inundation of worldly waters in the flood.

But what that fire will be and whence it will come, Hieronymus Magius disputes in On the Burning of the World book 3: yet we love Augustine's modesty, who in the place praised judges that no one, so far as he himself knows, has known these things. But here it is controverted whether the starry heaven also is to be purged by fire. The most ancient fathers affirm it. Augustine denies it, and with him the juniors. We hold the ancients' sentence, resting on the sayings of Scripture by which we have already proved that this world will perish, to be preferable to the other.

title: Augustine's doubt on the heavens; Greeks and Latins before him affirm corruption of the heavens
english: Augustine dissents (City of God book 20, chapter 24), and speaking doubtfully on Psalm 101: There are, he says, three heavens of heavens superior in the firmament. But whether they themselves also will perish by fire, or only those heavens which also perished in the flood, is a somewhat more scrupulous debate among the learned; nor can it easily be explained, especially in the narrowness of time. But how many now follow Augustine's sentence, Sixtus of Siena shows (Sacred Library book 6, annotation 246) and Feuardentius on Irenaeus book 4, chapter 6.

Against whom you will set the fathers, both all the Greeks and the Latins who wrote before Augustine — namely Justin Martyr, or whoever else, in the Confutation of Aristotle's Dogmas book 2 On the Heavens denying that the heavens can be corrupted; Irenaeus book 4, chapter 6; Ambrose Hexaemeron book 1, chapter 6; and among juniors also Augustinus Eugubinus on 2 Peter 3; and Hieronymus Magius On the Burning of the World book 2, chapters 6 and 7.

title: II. Whether the world perishes as to substance or only qualities is uncertain; commoner opinion: renovation
english: II. Whether this world will truly perish as to substance, or only as to its qualities, is uncertain. The more common sentence is that the world will not simply perish but is to be renewed, and Paul strongly urges this (Romans 8:19, 20, 21, 22), and because new heavens and a new earth are often mentioned in the Scriptures.

The ancients, whose sentences Gerhard Vossius, a man of diffuse learning — whose works we cite here gathers as it were in a medley (disputation On the End of the World, thesis 3, page 280), all thought that this world will not utterly perish but is to be renewed: as Irenaeus, Andrew of Caesarea, Probus in Epiphanius, Eusebius, Philastrius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret, Aeneas of Gaza, Elias of Crete on Gregory of Nazianzus's tenth oration, Basil the emperor Constantine, Oecumenius, Euthymius. From the Latins: Hilary, Jerome, Quintus Julius Hilarianus, Augustine, Julian of Toledo, Bede, Alcuin, Ambrosius Ansbertus, Olympiodorus, Haymo, Anselm or Hervaeus Brito, Peter Lombard, Otto of Freising, Hugh Etherianus, Hildegard, Vincent of Beauvais, Nicholas of Lyra, Ludolph the Saxon Carthusian, and others.

title: Juniors who hold substance-perishing; Chassanis; we prefer renovation yet dare not harshly reject
english: Certain of the juniors dissent from all these, namely Johannes Chassanis, a French theologian (Common Places book 3, chapter 22). Revelation 20:14 and 21:1 seem to favor his sentence, where it is expressly said that the sea will be no more; also Psalm 102:27–28; Luke 21:33; Job 14:12; Psalm 72:7. For this reason we dare not reject harshly the sentence of those who judge that the world will perish according to substance — especially since nothing about it was defined of old by any synod, and certain truly outstanding men dissent about it. Meanwhile we more approve the former sentence.

title: III. The precise time of the conflagration is unknown; always prepare by watching, prayer, repentance
english: III. Nor is it more certain to humans when this world's conflagration will definitely and precisely be future, so that, security shaken off, they may always prepare themselves for it by watching, praying, and performing the exercises of repentance.

For wisely Augustine (City of God book 18, chapter 53): It is altogether importune, he says, that that be asked. And he adds: If it were profitable for us to know this, by whom better than by God's own Master would it be said to the asking disciples? For they were not silent about it before him, but asked of him present, saying, Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? But he: It is not yours, he says, to know the times which the Father has put in his own power (Acts 1:6–7). They had certainly not asked about day or hour or year, but about the time, when they received that answer. So also Anastasius of Sinai (Hexaemeron book 7): The true exit and end of the age, he says, only the creator of times and of all things knows. And Vincent of Beauvais (Natural Mirror book 32, chapter 102): How much time remains until the end of the age, it is certain that no mortal knows, unless perhaps the Lord has revealed it to someone by special grace. For he who says It is not yours to know commands the fingers of all who calculate about this matter to rest.

title: Against mathematicians' great year and the rabbinic six-thousand-year scheme ascribed to Elijah
english: Therefore certain mathematicians and philosophers are in vain who say that it will be in the great year, within which the sun, moon, and all the stars return to the same place of heaven whence they set out; on which see Censorinus On the Birthday chapter 18. The opinion of the Jews and of certain fathers also seems propped on uncertain conjectures — that the world will last six thousand years: two before the law, two under the law, two after the law under the Messiah. That this was said by Elijah the Tishbite has been believed not only by Jews but by many of the Christians, as by Stratonicus bishop of Cumae, as Sixtus of Siena proves from his collectanea (Sacred Library book 2, under Elias), who himself also seems to have been of that sentence, and also Ludovicus Vives (City of God book 20, chapter 7).

We confess indeed that it is Elijah's — but not the Tishbite's, but a Cabbalist Rabbi's, whose comment, as Genebrard observes at the start of his Chronography, is read in the Talmud, in the treatise Sanhedrin and in the treatise On Idolatry and in the treatise On the Sabbath.

title: Rabbi Isaac's four reasons for six millennia; juniors' additions from Genesis 6, Moses, Jericho, Esdras, Apocalypse
english: The reasons by which the Rabbis defend the truth of this saying, Rabbi Isaac on Genesis chapter 1 offers four. (1) Because the first verse of Genesis contains א six times, by which a thousand is denoted. (2) Because God made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh; but a thousand years before God are as one day. (3) Because God, both in days and in years, indicates by the sixfold the time of labor and by the sevenfold the time of rest. For he commanded us to work six days and on the seventh to rest from all work: he also granted a six-year period to agriculture, but in the seventh year enjoined rest both on the field and on the cultivator. (4) Because the six first makers of the human race died — namely Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalalel, Jared — but Enoch, who is the seventh, happily translated into a place known to God, still lives.

To which reasons some of the juniors add: (5) Because when the human race was corrupted God said (Genesis 6:3), My spirit will not remain in man forever, for he is flesh: and his days will be one hundred twenty years — where first they understand the time of repentance granted before the flood, which was 120; if you take it fifty times, the number of six thousand results. (6) They also gather the same from Moses' age. For he lived 120 years (Deuteronomy 34:7): forty years in Pharaoh's court (Acts 7:23), forty in exile with Jethro (Exodus 2:15 and 3:1), by which two thousand years under the law are adumbrated; likewise he ruled the Israelite people forty years in the desert (Exodus 16:35), by which two thousand years under Messiah's empire are signified. (7) To these they add that Noah's ark rested in the seventh month (Genesis 8:4); that Moses was in the cloud six days and on the seventh was called by the Lord (Exodus 24:16); that when the Israelites had gone around Jericho six days, on the seventh day its walls fell (Joshua 6:16); likewise that the angel foretold to Esdras (4 Esdras 7:30) that the age would be of seven days; further that seven trumpets (Revelation 8:2) and seven bowls (Revelation 16:1) are commemorated, and certain other things of the same kind. Therefore what Christ said to the Apostles present, let us think said also to us: It is not yours to know the times which the Father has put in his own power (Acts 1:7).

title: IV. Scripture reveals the last day as not far; signs of Christ's approach — Jews' conversion, gospel preaching
english: IV. But God has revealed in Scripture an indefinite time of the last day, and various things signify that it is not so very remote from this our age. Some declare simply that Christ's advent is approaching; others are immediately joined with Christ's advent. Of the former mark are: (1) the conversion of the Jews predicted (Romans 11:25; Revelation 3:9 and 7:4–8) — see Finus Hadrianus in The Scourge of the Jews book 7, chapter 20; (2) the preaching of the Gospel through the whole world, as Augustine wills (letters 78 and 80 to Hesychius), Jerome on Matthew chapter 24, Origen tractate 28 on Matthew, Prosper's reply to the fourth chapter of the Gauls, Ambrose on Luke book 10, the author of the Incomplete Work homily 48 on Matthew, Damascene On the Orthodox Faith book 4, chapter 27. From the more recent: Lyra, Cajetan, Maldonatus on Matthew 24, Bellarmine On the Roman Pontiff book 3, chapter 4, Suarez disputation 50, tome 2.

title: Signs in sun, earth, and sea; Jewish fifteen signs; disputed sign of the cross; sign of the Son of Man
english: Of the latter mark are things in the world, in which both heaven is beheld and the globe of earth and sea (Luke 21:25–26). On the Scriptures and Ecclesiastical Dogmas book 3, tractate 3, folio 159. The Jews hand down fifteen signs which will precede the last day by fifteen days, which Thomas recounts from Jerome (Sentences book 4, distinction 48, question 1, article 4). But that they assign to each sign its own day is Rabbinic.

Hither they also refer that the sign of the cross will appear in heaven, and they gather that from Matthew 24:30. Remaclus de Vaulx in Divine Harpocrates or On the Consummation of the World part 2: By this sign, he says, both Greeks and Latins with consenting minds assert that Christ's cross is signified. And Lucas Pinellus On the Other Life book 2, chapter 20: By this sign of the Son of Man, he says, all interpreters, both Greek and Latin, affirm that the cross is signified. Whom Maldonatus refutes on Matthew chapter 24. It seems simpler if the sign of the Son of Man is understood as the Son of Man himself coming in a cloud (Luke 21:27), whose sight will be the most certain sign of the world's end. By a similar phrase the sign of circumcision is taken for circumcision itself (Romans 4:11). See the ocean of antiquity and learning, Gerhard Johann Vossius, disputation On the Advent of Christ, theses 5–9.

title: V. Since the world and its goods will soon perish, cling not; Christian wisdom dismisses the world — Cap. 6 close
english: V. Since this world with all its goods will soon perish and cannot grant perpetual quiet and tranquillity to our mind, it is extreme madness and misery so to cling to it that by love of it you lose the true good; but it belongs to Christian wisdom and felicity in this life to send a farewell to the world and its goods, so that after this life you may enjoy the eternal good. Hither looks Paul's warning (1 Corinthians 7:29, 30, 31) and David's (Psalm 49:4, 7, 12, 13, 15, 20, 21).
